about.title: Exeter Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Exeter is a small Tulare County community, and many residents rely on nearby clinics, urgent care, and regional hospitals for everything from routine checkups to emergency treatment. Most visits go fine, but sometimes a diagnosis is missed, a medication is mishandled, or a surgical step goes wrong, and a patient is left dealing with harm that never should have happened. California law treats these situations differently than a routine injury claim, with its own notice requirements and evidence standards, which is why getting the right guidance matters. LawProactive doesn't practice law or decide your case; we simply help Exeter patients and families get in touch with an independent attorney who can look honestly at what happened. If a provider's care fell below the accepted standard and caused real harm, that conversation costs nothing to start, and there's no obligation to move forward until you're ready.

whyChoose.title: What Exeter Patients Should Know About California Malpractice Law

items.title: Strict, Layered Deadlines
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from when you discover the harm, but never more than three years from the injury itself, to bring a claim. Missing either window can end a case before it starts, so early guidance matters.

items.title: A 90-Day Notice Comes First
items.desc: Before a lawsuit can be filed, California law requires sending the provider a 90-day notice of intent. An attorney familiar with this step can help make sure it's handled correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Almost Always Required
items.desc: A poor outcome by itself isn't proof of malpractice; California generally requires a qualified medical expert to confirm the standard of care was breached. This is a key reason to have knowledgeable counsel evaluate the medical records early.

items.question: I had a bad outcome after treatment in Exeter — does that mean it was malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law recognizes that medicine carries inherent risk, so a poor result alone isn't enough to prove malpractice. What matters is whether the provider's care fell below the accepted medical standard, which is why a qualified expert review is almost always needed.

items.question: How long do I have to act on a malpractice claim in California?
items.answer: Generally you have one year from when you discover, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury, but no more than three years from the date it occurred. There's also a required 90-day pre-suit notice to the provider before filing, so timelines can move quickly once you decide to act.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: Yes, California places a statutory cap on non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases, though that cap rises each year under current law. Economic losses like medical bills and lost income are generally handled separately from that cap.

items.question: Does LawProactive handle malpractice claims involving Exeter clinics directly?
items.answer: No, LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm, so we don't handle or evaluate claims ourselves. We simply help you reach an independent attorney who can review what happened at the Exeter facility involved and advise you on next steps.
